title: Passover: a candle and a feather
hookLine: the night before, a search for leaven by candlelight

lines: A CANDLE, A FEATHER, A SPOON.
cards: It's the night before Passover. The house has been cleaned for weeks. The kitchen is scrubbed; the counters are covered.
And now the lights go off. A parent lights a single candle. A child holds a feather and a wooden spoon.

Somebody else carries a paper bag. They walk slowly through the dark house, room by room, peering under the couch and along the windowsills. And here's the funny part: everyone knows what they'll find.
Earlier, someone hid a few little pieces of bread around the house, wrapped so they won't leave crumbs. The search is real, and it's also a kind of game.

teach.b: Bedikat chametz means the search for leaven. The Mishnah opens its tractate on Passover with it: on the night of the fourteenth of Nisan, one searches for chametz by the light of a lamp. Why at night, and why a candle?

teach.h: A CANDLE GOES INTO THE CRACKS.
teach.b: The Talmud says night is when people are home, and a small flame is better than daylight for this job, because you can carry it into holes and cracks where sunlight never reaches.
A torch is too big and scary to bring close. So: one candle, close up. The Talmud also finds verses about searching with lamps.

teach.h: THE LAMP OF THE LORD SEARCHES.
teach.b: One is from Proverbs, in the old Jewish translation: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD, searching all the inward parts."
The rabbis set it beside the night search: a candle moving through the house, and the lamp the proverb says searches a person. The feather sweeps the crumbs into the spoon.
The hidden pieces are a later custom, so the search never comes up empty and the blessing said before it isn't wasted.

teach.h: WHAT YOU MISSED IS LIKE DUST.
teach.b: When it's done, the family says a short Aramaic declaration: any leaven I haven't seen or found is nullified, ownerless, like the dust of the earth. In the morning, what was collected is burned.
Then comes the honest part. You searched carefully, and you'll still miss something. Jewish law expects that, and the declaration covers it.
The search asks for real attention, and then forgives you for being human.

how: On the night before Passover, families say a blessing and search the house for chametz by candlelight, often with a feather and wooden spoon and a few hidden pieces of bread, then recite the Aramaic nullification and burn the chametz the next morning.

games.q: you're searching the house for chametz. you could use a bright torch, a single candle, or wait for morning sunlight. which does the Talmud prefer?
games.why: a candle: small enough to bring close, into holes and cracks, where a torch is too big and daylight doesn't reach.

practice: If you like, light a candle or dim the lights, and bring your attention close, like a small flame, to one corner of your life you don't usually look at: a habit, a resentment, an unanswered message.
Don't fix it yet; just see it clearly, the way a candle shows a crumb. Then let go of what you can't find tonight.

wordCard.voice: Bedikat chametz. The search for leaven, by candlelight, on the night before Passover. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: search by candle. What you miss is counted as dust. Day six hundred seventy-seven, done.
